cim: Symphony Review: A Team of AI Agents for the Business Behind Your Website
cim_eredeti: Symphony Review: A Team of AI Agents for the Business Behind Your Website
szoveg_eredeti:
To be a small business owner is to spin multiple plates at once: lead generation, client outreach, general marketing and sales, design, and much more. Often, some of those plates will fall and smash, which might mean you lose a good prospect, don’t hit a deadline, or myriad other negatives.

By the end of this Symphony review, you might choose to take a breath and let its Maestro orchestrator organize your work tasks, so you can sweep up the broken crockery!

Each of Symphony’s four pricing tiers comes with the core functionality of Maestro and the ability to use multiple AI agents around the clock.

The difference between each plan is the number of AI credits you receive per month, the ‘activity level’ of your agents, the number of actions you have available, and your usage allocation. Here are the three premium plans:

The cost I give here is based on annual billing. A month-by-month subscription costs slightly more. There aren’t any exact figures on the activity level of your agents and usage allocation either, just that higher tiers give you more.

Free is more of an extended taster of what Symphony can give you. There’s an allocation of 500 credits per month and 100 daily credits. I think the Free plan is a generous offering given what’s included in the premium tiers. You also get two agent actions and briefings.

If your credits run out before the month’s end, agents pause the work and wait for your credit allocation. It means you won’t need to adapt to an unfinished workflow or lose any work.

If you run a small business, there are a few concerns you likely have regularly:

This is what Symphony aims to improve. In a nutshell, you chat with Maestro (the orchestrator) and after it learns about your business, it dishes out the work to a set of AI agents.

Each agent has one area of responsibility, but you can add custom agents if you need to work on a specific task. Wix claims the agent knowledge comes from 300 million businesses across a variety of regions and industries.

Symphony is platform-agnostic, which means you don’t need to run a Wix site to use it (although you do need a Wix account). Instead, it connects to your calendars, email account, CRM, MCP server, and other tools.

My first impression is that Symphony is going to be most helpful for single-person businesses or small teams. Freelancers or content creators fit the bill, but agencies that run several projects at once can also benefit.

The Pro plan is likely the best fit for all of these business types. A freelancer with a small workload could opt for Basic, but you wouldn’t want to restrict your growth based on your Symphony plan.

There are four core aspects to Symphony that cover the majority of your needs:

Everything works through human-language prompts, and each project gets its own contained workspace. For instance, you can tell Maestro the details of your business and it assembles a team of AI agents based on the suitability for the task. It covers outreach and marketing, scheduling, research, design, and even finance.

The information is also used to build a knowledge base, which involves a constant learning cycle. Part of the allure of Symphony is that the results should get better as Maestro accumulates more knowledge.

All considered, the guardrails and scope mean Symphony is a safe solution. However, you can’t set and forget anything, as you still need to oversee the work Maestro does. The approval system keeps that scope fixed in place.

Before I get into a walkthrough of Symphony, I want to quickly go over how it connects to a WordPress website. In fact, a site connection only matters if you need agents to edit or read your site’s content.

Symphony’s scope is based on whether you self-host WordPress or use WordPress.com. A typical self-hosted WordPress site will need to use Jetpack to then connect to the WordPress.com MCP server, although this doesn’t need a premium Jetpack account.

I’m using the desktop version of Symphony here, but you can also download the mobile app from the Google Play Store or Apple’s App Store. Once you sign up, you’ll need to answer some questions about your business to help kick start Maestro.

Next, you can choose to connect some of your essential business tools, although the Wix documentation calls this “optional”. I’d suggest you connect something, such as your email account. Make sure it’s relevant to your goals for using Symphony. You can ask Maestro, but also head to Settings > Connectors and MCPs in Symphony:

You can begin chatting with Maestro about the goals you need to achieve from any page using the bottom toolbar. However, the Home screen gives you some inspiration and guidance:

You can begin a chat here, or browse any of the other pages. For instance, Chats lists all of the conversations you’ve had with Maestro so far.

One of my Symphony chats warns me about a WordPress exploit that may need patching. That’s a nice touch.

When it comes to documentation, you can find Symphony content within the main Wix Help Center.

There are only a few articles here, but not all cover using Symphony. The rest look at choosing a plan and AI credit usage. I’d expect the details on choosing your plan to be on a sales page rather than here. Plus, that information repeats what’s on the main Symphony page anyway.

The main Using the App guide is short. I’m someone who wants to ‘read the manual’ before I use a tool, but you may want to dive in and test things out. I liked the depth of the AI credits page though. It helped me understand usage better than before, which might help if you want to dive in and spend a few credits trying things out.

Using the App also details the scope and escalation of support. First, you’d ask Maestro. I’m not excited by this as you’d likely want to step away from the tool that’s causing you an issue in the first place. However, Maestro can email support on your behalf, which is neat.

If you head to your account settings, you can message the customer care team directly. I’d rather do this by default, so it would be nice to see that option available and prominent.

I’m a WordPress user, so I didn’t want to set up a whole Wix site to test out Symphony. That’s an unfounded worry though, as Symphony is platform-agnostic and simple to initiate. It’s a simple premise – agentic AI organized as a team by an AI orchestrator – but it’s what many small businesses need.

I’m pleasantly surprised at what I could do with the functionality. Overall, I think Symphony has enough in the box to help you with those time-critical tasks you can’t seem to complete.

Is my Symphony review giving you a reason to sign up? I’d love to hear your thoughts in the comments section below!
